title: Slab Management, Long-Context Burst Resilience - Auriga Satellite Deep Dive
summary: Detailed technical workshop on slab-based KV cache behavior for long-context satellite telemetry use cases. Walkthrough of current eviction behavior, scenarios that cause paging during bursty long-context requests, analysis of prefix reuse patterns, and concrete suggestions (playbook) for tuning slab sizes, prefetch thresholds, and batching windows. Agreed next steps include running a 2h replay test with modified slab ratios and sharing prefetched telemetry traces and a bench spreadsheet.

transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-07-28 10:00 PDT, Duration: 1h8m, Recording id ff-20260728-auriga-slab-0371
Attendees: Ethan Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marco Liu (Redwood Infra), Lana Ortiz (Auriga ML), Ravi Patel (Auriga Platform), Sasha Kim (Auriga SRE), Tom Becker (Auriga CTO)

---- Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect) ----
Redwood walked through slab allocation model differences between fixed-shard slabs and adaptive compaction. Focus on sporadic long-context requests from ground-station telemetry pipelines that produce bursts of 20-60s sequences causing KV slab paging and increased token latency. Discussed hotkey/prefix detection to avoid global spill and tradeoffs of increasing per-slab quota vs. overall memory footprint. Touched on quantization effects on KV size and on-prem VPC disk I/O limits affecting spill latency.

---- Topics covered ----
- Slab sizing, per-prefix isolation, eviction signatures
- Paging vs eviction: when we spill to disk and how we reclaim
- Long-context bursts: KV growth patterns, KV prefix reuse vs new-session churn
- Batching interaction: smaller micro-batches prevent clog but reduce throughput
- On-prem constraints: NFS latency and burst IO limits; KMS and audit log considerations briefly
- Quick demo of simulated replay showing slab thrash at 1200 concurrent prefixes

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about an hour, hour ten. We'll do a short rundown then Priya will walk through the slab model and a replay trace we prepared.
[00:18] Lana (Auriga): Thanks. We have a couple of folks from infra on, cause we've totally hit a pain point last week where our inference pipeline saw a 2x latency spike for long context sessions.
[00:28] Priya (Redwood): Yeah and that's exactly what we want to dig into; we mapped out the KV growth pattern from your traces and there's a few signatures that look like slab saturations followed by paging.
[00:35] Ravi (Auriga): Quick note on topology: we're on-prem in a VPC-like setup, storage is NFS-backed SSDs and we have a 5Gbps egress cap on the node group.
[00:47] Marco (Redwood): That matters because spillback latency is mostly network+disk. If the slab spills to disk, the round trip is not just IO, it's routing.
[00:55] Sasha (Auriga): Right; and our ops alarm only fires on error rates not on subtle token-latency increases so it took a while to notice.

[01:05] Priya: Ok I'm sharing the replay clip: this is a 30-minute window where there are oscillating long-context burst sessions. Timestamps in the traces align with the big token spikes. Notice around t+12m we have sustained KV growth.
[01:21] (screen share noise)
[01:25] Priya: So our runtime uses slab-based KV allocation: each prefix gets a small preferred slab and if usage exceeds that, we either evict oldest entries for that prefix or spill to shared slab pool depending on policy. The problem is when many prefixes become hot concurrently.
[01:40] Lana: Is that the standard fixed slab config? We didn't change anything recently.
[01:44] Priya: Looks like you were on the default production profile where slab ratios are 60/30/10 (per-prefix/pooled/compaction reserve). For your workload the hot-prefix cardinality is high, so the pooled slab saturates quickly and eviction starts to hop prefixes.
[01:58] Ravi: And by hop you mean we evict from different prefixes unpredictably?
[02:02] Priya: Correct. Eviction becomes non-local; instead of reclaiming from the offending prefix we pull from the pooled slab which may contain other active prefixes. That causes prefix reuse to miss and re-population thrashes.

[02:12] Tom (Auriga): Could we just raise the per-prefix quota? I mean, give each prefix more headroom.
[02:17] Marco: You can, but it's linear to memory. Two considerations: one, memory is finite — raising per-prefix decreases pooled headroom for bursts; two, it can hide the underlying burst pattern rather than fix IO pressure.
[02:30] Ethan: Also remember quantized KV entries are smaller, but quantization here is of activations vs of stored keys; your current quantized model reduces token size by ~25% but not evenly across prefixes, so slab bookkeeping still spikes.

[02:46] Sasha: On the spill side, we saw spikes in write latency to NFS at the same time as token latency; is that correlated?
[02:52] Priya: Highly correlated. When the pooled slab overflows we page to local disk (or remote NFS depending on node config). For on-prem you said NFS, so we saw remote writes amplify the latency.
[03:00] Lana: So is the immediate action to make slabs bigger or to change where we spill?
[03:06] Priya: There are a few levers. I'll list them briefly: 1) Adjust per-prefix slab ratio to favor more per-prefix headroom for high-cardinality workloads; 2) Increase compaction reserve to reduce how often we run compaction — careful tradeoff; 3) Turn on hotkey detection + prefix pinning to keep very hot prefixes off the pooled slab; 4) Tune prefetch thresholds so we avoid greedily prefetching large long-context caches during bursts.

[03:30] Ravi: Hotkey detection — does it rely on counting within the runtime or does it need external telemetry?
[03:34] Priya: Runtime-local counters are sufficient for ephemeral detection. We keep an LFU-ish counter per prefix and if a prefix crosses a hot threshold it gets pinned to per-prefix slab. There is a small CPU overhead but usually worth it.
[03:45] Tom: Pinning sounds promising. Any downside?
[03:47] Marco: Downsides: possible starvation for other prefixes if many get pinned; also pinning is sticky for configured TTLs. We prefer dynamic unpin based on decay windows.

[04:00] Ethan: Let me show the replay where we simulated pinning on-the-fly. (screen) You can see the token latency line drops and pooled slab pressure plateaus.
[04:12] Lana: Nice — but I see a secondary hump later around t+22m. What's that?
[04:16] Priya: That hump is the refill effect — pinned prefixes maintain KV, but new long-context sessions create entries that still need pooled space; if your incoming cardinality keeps growing, pool will hit cap regardless. That's where prefetch backpressure and batching windows matter.

[04:35] Sasha: Explain batching windows; we've been told to lower GPU batch size to reduce tail latency, but that lowered throughput.
[04:42] Priya: Right. There's two batching layers: runtime request batching for GPU execution and KV batching for prefetch population. For KV, if you increase population window (aggregate more prefixes before sending prefetches) you can reduce IO spikes but increase cold-start for some requests. It's a latency vs throughput tradeoff.
[04:58] Ravi: Can we just stagger prefetches? Like random jitter to avoid thundering herd?
[05:01] Priya: Yes, jittered prefetch and backoff thresholds are part of the playbook. We also suggest a token-budget-based prefetch: limit total prefetched tokens per-second to a cap derived from your observed steady-state throughput.

[05:18] Tom: Any recommendations specific to NFS?
[05:20] Marco: For NFS-backed spills: 1) ensure sticky local caching where feasible; 2) prefer batched writes over many small writes — small writes kill throughput; 3) set a node-level IO throttle to avoid saturating your network egress which causes cross-node latency in our spill paths.

[05:36] Lana: Priya earlier mentioned compaction reserve tweaks — can you expand?
[05:39] Priya: Yeah, compaction reserve is a reserved slab chunk we use to compact hot entries out of pooled slab before spilling. Increasing reserve reduces immediate spills but it also increases memory reservation. For your workload we've seen improvements when reserve is bumped from 10% to 18% with a proportional smaller pooled slab. It cut paging events by ~40% in sim, but memory headroom decreased.

[05:58] Ethan: We'll attach the simulation config and the bench spreadsheet. There's a sheet that models memory headroom vs expected concurrent prefixes; you can plug in your cardinality and burst profiles.

[06:08] Priya: One more nuance: quantization of KV data. If you enable 4-bit quantization for activations the serialized KV size drops but CPU time to dequantize increases slightly on spills. On remote spilled reads, dequant time adds to overall token latency. For on-prem with slow NFS, keeping KV unquantized on-disk may actually be faster because decompression code path is cheaper than remote transfer. Weird, but we've seen it.

[06:33] Ravi: So compression/quantization isn't always win for spills. We need to test.

[06:36] Marco: Exactly. We recommend toggling quantization only after you measure spill IO profiles and include dequant CPU cost in the model.

[06:45] (brief silence, background typing)

[06:52] Priya: Ok I'm jumping to the simulated flame graph from Wednesday's replay — look at the timeline where eviction rate spikes at high cardinality. There's a clear correlation between the pooled slab high watermark crossing and the token tail 95->99th percentile.
[07:10] Lana: Any heuristics to detect impending thrash proactively?
[07:13] Priya: We recommend two signals: rate of new prefix allocations per-second, and growth rate of pooled slab usage. If new prefix allocations exceed a configured threshold and pooled growth is above X% in Y seconds, trigger a throttling response — e.g., reduce prefetch aggression or switch to strict per-prefix capping temporarily.
[07:33] Sasha: Could we push alerts to our Grafana? We want a runbook entry too.
[07:37] Ethan: Absolutely — we'll provide example Prometheus rules and a runbook snippet. We'll include alert thresholds from the bench.

[07:45] Tom: What about the interplay with routing for dedicated vs hosted? We want the option to fallback to a smaller hosted model if on-prem saturates. Does Redwood support auto-routing?
[07:54] Priya: Yes, smart routing can fallback to a lower-memory model or hosted endpoint. But the decision latency means you'll still see user-perceived slowdown during the failover. It's better as graceful degradation than as primary mitigation.

[08:08] Ravi: For the DR plan, our legal folks want logs/audit of spilled keys. Any PII concerns?
[08:14] Marco: On spill we can apply deterministic redaction and ensure KMS wrapping for disk encryption. We'll share the security doc for on-prem. This is standard but we need to validate your compliance needs.

[08:26] Priya: Back to tuning: here's a short playbook we recommend for your stack (high-level) — order matters: 1) enable hotkey detection and pin highly active prefixes; 2) increase compaction reserve slightly (10->18%); 3) add jittered prefetch and token-budget cap; 4) run a 2h replay with these settings and capture IO metrics; 5) if paging persists, consider increasing physical memory or moving spill to faster local SSDs instead of NFS.

[08:55] Lana: That seems actionable. For step 1, how quickly do pins propagate in a multi-node cluster?
[08:59] Priya: Pins are local decisions but replicated to cluster control plane within a second. We had a scenario with cross-node consistency lags; in those cases we fall back to conservative eviction policies until control plane confirms.

[09:13] Ravi: Can the control plane be hosted or do we need to host it on-prem?
[09:16] Ethan: Both. For Private deployment you can run the control plane inside your VPC. That reduces cross-site latency for decisions but increases ops burden. We'll include deployment pros/cons in the doc.

[09:27] Tom: Any quick mitigation we can flip tonight to reduce risk?
[09:30] Priya: Short term: reduce prefetch aggressiveness and enable jittered prefetch. That should lower IO spikes without much impact on average latency. Change is config-only and reversible.

[09:40] Sasha: Great. We'll try that in the canary pool.

[09:44] (brief keyboard clack)

[09:47] Priya: I also want to call out a subtle metric: prefix reuse rate. If prefix reuse is low, prefetch gives little value because you're prefetching entries that won't get reused. So compute a reuse ratio: reused_entries / total_prefetched. If it's below ~0.25, reduce prefetch.

[10:02] Lana: How do we measure reuse ratio in our traces?
[10:05] Priya: We can instrument to tag prefetched entries with ephemeral IDs and then correlate. It's in the playbook. We'll provide a lightweight Prom exporter.

[10:12] Ethan: Ok let's go over the action items and owners — then we can open the floor for questions.

[10:20] (Auriga folks ask some clarifying Qs)
[10:22] Ravi: Regarding instrumentation: does Redwood need access to raw traces? We prefer anonymized aggregates.
[10:26] Marco: Aggregates are fine; we only need prefix cardinality distributions and per-node IO latency histograms. The full trace helps but is not required.

[10:33] Tom: If we decide to change slab ratios permanently, what's the risk window? Could we create a worse churning scenario?
[10:38] Priya: If misconfigured, you could starve pooled slab causing more frequent remote spills. That's why we recommend staged ramping and replay testing. Start with small increments and run the bench.

[10:48] Lana: One more: any relation between tokenizer behavior and prefix explosion? We have sessions that split into many small prefixes because of tokenization differences.
[10:55] Priya: Yes tokenizer changes can increase prefix cardinality; we recommend normalizing prefix keys upstream (e.g., canonicalization) to reduce accidental cardinality inflation.

[11:05] Ethan: Ok final recap: Redwood sends playbook + prom rules + bench sheet (Ethan). Auriga runs 2h replay with new settings and returns telemetry (Ravi). Priya will prototype slab ratio changes locally and report. We'll reconvene in ~10 days.

[11:22] (meeting ends)
